title: Practice Set PMSI5 — Reading Production Memory Pipelines
description: Mid recognition track capstone: two production-style 50–55 line memory pipelines. Read line by line, answer 5 questions per pipeline about config, cache lifecycle, salt determinism, footprint, and re-execution cost. PMSI5.2 weaves five mid-level memory-and-skew bugs into one snippet.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Mid memory & skew scenarios reference NordGrid at mid production scale (12M meters across 12 regions, 24× the junior dataset).
Substations reference (~200 rows at mid scale). Anchors broadcast-eligibility scenarios.

tasks.title: Aggregation Pipeline With Memory Footprint Audit

description.context: A NordGrid mid-level engineer's daily-aggregation pipeline runs at production scale (12M meters). The senior engineer schedules a memory audit and walks through five targeted questions about the pipeline's memory footprint at each step.
description.task: Read the pipeline carefully — line numbers are shown — then answer all the questions below.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import (col, sum, broadcast, hash, concat,
                                     lit, abs as f_abs, split)

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName('billing_aggregation')
    .config('spark.executor.memory', '8g')
    .config('spark.executor.memoryOverhead', '1500m')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', '200')
    .getOrCreate())

# Step 1: load and filter
meters = spark.read.parquet('silver/meters/2026-04-30/')   # 12M rows
active = meters.filter(col('status') == 'ACTIVE')

# Step 2: salt customer_type to handle the 60/25/12/3 skew
#   (engineer chose salt factor 120 based on the 60% dominant share)
salted = active.withColumn('customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (f_abs(hash(col('meter_id'))) % 120).cast('int')))

# Step 3: aggregate at salted level (partial)
partial = salted.groupBy('customer_type_salted', 'region').agg(
    sum('daily_kw').alias('partial_kw'))
partial.cache()

# Step 4: enrich with substations (broadcast eligible)
subs = spark.read.parquet('reference/substations/')   # 200 rows
enriched = partial.join(broadcast(subs), on='region', how='left')

# Step 5: re-aggregate at customer_type level (final)
final = (enriched
    .withColumn('customer_type', split('customer_type_salted', '_')[0])
    .groupBy('customer_type', 'region', 'capacity_mw')
    .agg(sum('partial_kw').alias('total_kw')))

# Step 6: write
final.write.mode('overwrite').partitionBy('region').parquet('gold/billing/')

# Step 7: cleanup
print(f'Pipeline complete; {final.count()} aggregated rows')

fields.label: Q1 — Q1 — Lines 7-12 (the SparkSession configuration). Given no Python UDFs, a 200-row broadcast on line 30, and AQE enabled, is the configuration appropriate?
options: Wrong — spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled is not set explicitly. Without it, AQE only does skew handling, not partition coalescing on the post-shuffle output.
Wrong — spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled is not set. Without it, AQE only does skew handling, not partition coalescing. Add that config.
Wrong — 1500m overhead is wasteful for a JVM-only workload. Drop to default 800m to free container budget for compute and other allocations.
All settings here are reasonable for the described workload. 8g heap + 1500m overhead leaves room without UDFs. Adaptive execution + skewJoin are on.
fields.correctAnswer: All settings here are reasonable for the described workload. 8g heap + 1500m overhead leaves room without UDFs. Adaptive execution + skewJoin are on.
fields.rationale: Defaults align with this workload's profile.5+ when adaptive is enabled, so explicit setting is not required.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Miscomputes partition target.60K rows × 200 bytes = 12MB per task is fine.5+.
Option C: Treats overhead headroom as waste.

fields.label: Q2 — Q2 — Line 25 (`partial.cache()`). The pipeline uses `partial` exactly twice (line 30 join, line 38 final groupBy via `enriched`). Is the cache useful, and is there a lifecycle bug?
options: Useless — `partial` is referenced once. enriched is built from partial, then final from enriched. Single-pass lineage; cache adds executor pressure for no benefit.
Useful and there is no lifecycle bug; Spark auto-unpersists when the DataFrame falls out of scope. The engineer does not need to manage cache explicitly.
Useful — `partial` feeds two downstream steps. The lifecycle bug: .unpersist() is missing, so the cache lives until SparkSession ends, holding ~120MB across executors.
Wrong storage level — default MEMORY_ONLY cannot hold the partial result; switch to MEMORY_AND_DISK to allow disk fallback and avoid recomputation under pressure.
fields.correctAnswer: Useful — `partial` feeds two downstream steps. The lifecycle bug: .unpersist() is missing, so the cache lives until SparkSession ends, holding ~120MB across executors.
fields.rationale: Line 30's join consumes partial; line 38's de-salt re-aggregate consumes it again through enriched.Caching avoids re-running the salted partial.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Misreads the lineage; partial is consumed in two action paths.
Option B: Treats cache() as auto-cleaned.unpersist() or session end.

fields.label: Q3 — Q3 — Line 22 (the salt formula `f_abs(hash(col('meter_id'))) % 120`). What property does this salt have that the rand()-based version lacks?
options: Faster than rand() because hash() is JVM-native while rand() is Python-side. The performance gain matters at 12M rows because the salt is on the hot path.
Faster because hash() can be vectorized by Tungsten while rand() cannot; vectorization gives 2-3× speedup on the salt computation across 12M rows.
Correctly factored at 120 to match the 60% dominant share; the rand() version would be correct only if the dominant share were 30% or lower.
DETERMINISTIC — for a given meter_id, hash % 120 always returns the same bucket. The rand() version is non-deterministic across stage retries, leading to mismatched salts.
fields.correctAnswer: DETERMINISTIC — for a given meter_id, hash % 120 always returns the same bucket. The rand() version is non-deterministic across stage retries, leading to mismatched salts.
fields.rationale: Reproducibility under re-execution is the property that distinguishes the two salts.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks performance over correctness.
Option B: Cites Tungsten vectorization; both rand() and hash() can be vectorized.

fields.label: Q4 — Q4 — Line 38 (the final groupBy after de-salting). What is the memory footprint of this final aggregation?
options: Materializes the entire enriched DataFrame on the driver before aggregating; the driver heap (default 1g) cannot hold ~1M rows. Risk: driver OOM. Fix: .coalesce(1) before groupBy.
Triggers a global shuffle by (customer_type, region, capacity_mw); shuffle volume is dominated by the broadcast-joined substation data, which inflates `enriched` to ~50× the partial size.
No-op because partial_kw was already aggregated at the salted level; the post-de-salt aggregation just sums identical values per group. Memory cost is essentially zero.
Operates on enriched (~1.15M rows post-partial-step + broadcast join). The reduction collapses back to ~9,600 rows. Footprint is small. Risk: substation count multiplication if the dim grew.
fields.correctAnswer: Operates on enriched (~1.15M rows post-partial-step + broadcast join). The reduction collapses back to ~9,600 rows. Footprint is small. Risk: substation count multiplication if the dim grew.
fields.rationale: Partial aggregation produces ~5,760 rows (4 customer_types × 120 salts × ~12 regions).Broadcast join with substations fans out modestly.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats groupBy as driver-side; it is executor-side via shuffle.
Option B: Over-estimates broadcast inflation.

fields.label: Q5 — Q5 — Line 47 (`final.count()`). What is the memory cost?
options: Free — count() returns a single Long; memory is negligible regardless of input size. The line is harmless and contributes nothing measurable to runtime.
Reads from `partial.cache()` on line 25, so the cost is only the de-salt re-aggregate plus count itself. Audit signal: Storage tab shows partial cache hits.
Forces re-execution because final is not cached. Cost: full pipeline re-run including salted partial, broadcast join, and de-salt re-aggregate. Audit: SQL tab shows TWO query executions.
Forces a global shuffle because count must coordinate across executors via the driver; small volume but latency dominated by waiting for the slowest executor.
fields.correctAnswer: Forces re-execution because final is not cached. Cost: full pipeline re-run including salted partial, broadcast join, and de-salt re-aggregate. Audit: SQL tab shows TWO query executions.
fields.rationale: `final` is NOT cached.count() triggers re-execution of the full lineage.count() on line 47.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats count() as universally free; uncached count re-executes the lineage.

tasks.title: The Pipeline With Five Mid-Level Memory-and-Skew Bugs

description.context: Final exercise of the Mid track. A NordGrid pipeline runs without errors but Finance reports billing arrives 4 hours late and Operations reports 'task failed 4 times' alerts. Investigation traces the symptoms to five distinct Mid-level memory-and-skew mistakes in the same 55-line pipeline.
description.task: Read the pipeline carefully — line numbers are shown — then answer all the questions below.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import (col, sum, broadcast, expr, lit,
                                     concat, split)

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName('billing')
    .config('spark.executor.memory', '8g')
    .config('spark.executor.memoryOverhead', '400m')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled', 'true')
    .config('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', '200')
    .config('spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold', '500m')
    .getOrCreate())

# Step 1: load
meters = spark.read.parquet('silver/meters/2026-04-30/')      # 12M rows
customers = spark.read.parquet('reference/customer_master/')  # 3M rows, 280MB

# Step 2: salt for skew (rand-based; salt factor 10)
salted_meters = meters.withColumn('customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'),
           (expr('rand() * 10').cast('int'))))

# Step 3: enrich with customer_master
enriched = salted_meters.join(broadcast(customers), on='customer_id', how='left')
enriched.cache()

# Step 4: outer-join to events for fraud detection
events = spark.read.parquet('silver/events/last_30_days/')   # 8M rows
flagged = enriched.join(events, on='meter_id', how='full_outer')

# Step 5: compute revenue (UDF over 12M rows)
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType

@udf(returnType=DoubleType())
def compute_revenue(daily_kw, customer_type, region):
    base = daily_kw * 0.18
    multiplier = {'RESIDENTIAL': 1.0, 'COMMERCIAL': 1.3,
                  'INDUSTRIAL': 1.5, 'PROSUMER': 0.85}.get(customer_type, 1.0)
    return base * multiplier

revenue = flagged.withColumn('revenue', compute_revenue(
    col('daily_kw'), col('customer_type_salted'), col('region')))

# Step 6: aggregate to per-region totals
summary = revenue.groupBy('region').agg(
    sum('revenue').alias('total_revenue_eur'))

summary.write.mode('overwrite').partitionBy('region').parquet('gold/billing/')

fields.label: Q1 — Bug #1 — Lines 7-8 (executor configuration) combined with the Python UDF on lines 39-43. What is the configuration mismatch?
options: Executor memory at 8g is too high for a workload with a Python UDF; the Python interpreter consumes JVM heap and OOMs. Fix: reduce --executor-memory to 4g to give Python more room outside the JVM.
Configuration is correct; 8g + 400m overhead is the standard NordGrid Mid setup for this scale. The bugs are in the salt logic, joins, and UDF — not in the SparkSession block at the top.
Off-heap budget at 400m is too small. The Python interpreter for the UDF grows to ~600MB-1GB on 12M rows; total RSS exceeds 8.4g and YARN kills the container. Raise overhead to 1500m.
spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=500m is dangerously high; broadcasting 280MB customer_master pressures the driver during build phase. Drop threshold to 10MB default.
fields.correctAnswer: Off-heap budget at 400m is too small. The Python interpreter for the UDF grows to ~600MB-1GB on 12M rows; total RSS exceeds 8.4g and YARN kills the container. Raise overhead to 1500m.
fields.rationale: The Python interpreter that runs PySpark UDFs consumes overhead memory, NOT heap.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Inverts heap-vs-overhead.Python lives in overhead, not heap.
Option B: Dismisses 400m as adequate.5g+ overhead.

fields.label: Q2 — Bug #2 — Lines 19-22 (the rand()-based salt). What is the bug, given AQE is enabled?
options: rand() is non-deterministic. AQE may re-evaluate the salting expression with new values. The salt mismatches against any downstream join. Fix: pmod(crc32(meter_id), 10).
rand()×10 returns Double 0-9.999; cast to Int gives 0-9. Bug: rand() seeds differently per executor, so the same meter_id can land in different buckets across re-runs.
rand() is correct here because the pipeline uses LEFT/FULL_OUTER joins; AQE skew handling does not engage on outer joins anyway. The bug is elsewhere.
rand()×10 produces a Double; concatenating to String introduces locale-dependent formatting (decimal separator). Salt strings are inconsistent across executors and miss matches.
fields.correctAnswer: rand() is non-deterministic. AQE may re-evaluate the salting expression with new values. The salt mismatches against any downstream join. Fix: pmod(crc32(meter_id), 10).
fields.rationale: Non-determinism in the salting expression is what the AQE-enabled cluster surfaces.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents per-executor rand() seeding.
Option C: Dismisses determinism because outer joins are used.

fields.label: Q3 — Bug #3 — Line 25 (`broadcast(customers)`) given customers is 280MB and threshold is 500m. What is the bug?
options: broadcast() forces materialization on the driver before broadcasting. Default 1g driver heap; 280MB inflates as a hashed relation to ~600MB. Remove the hint to let AQE downgrade if needed.
The hint is correct because customers (280MB) is below the 500m threshold; Catalyst will broadcast successfully without driver risk. There is no bug.
The hint is wrong because customers is the LEFT side of the join (joined to salted_meters from the left); broadcast hints only work on the right side. Swap join order.
The hint conflicts with AQE — AQE downgrades broadcast to sort-merge if conditions change, defeating the engineer's intent. Disable AQE for this stage.
fields.correctAnswer: broadcast() forces materialization on the driver before broadcasting. Default 1g driver heap; 280MB inflates as a hashed relation to ~600MB. Remove the hint to let AQE downgrade if needed.
fields.rationale: The hint commits Catalyst to broadcasting customers.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Overlooks driver-side risk under concurrent load.
Option C: Invents a right-side-only rule for broadcast hints.

fields.label: Q4 — Bug #4 — Line 32 (`flagged = enriched.join(events, on='meter_id', how='full_outer')`). Given 'task failed 4 times' alerts, what is the bug?
options: FULL OUTER is not supported by AQE skew handling. Customer_type is pre-skewed; FULL OUTER produces hot partitions AQE cannot split. Executors OOM, tasks fail 4 times. Fix: INNER + null-handling.
Join on meter_id but meters and events have different distributions (events 30 days vs meters 1 day); join produces row inflation. Fix: filter events by date before the join.
FULL OUTER joins are slower than INNER but produce no specific OOM risk; the 'task failed 4 times' alert is environmental noise unrelated to the join structure on this line.
FULL OUTER joins always shuffle both sides regardless of AQE; shuffle volume is 12M + 8M = 20M rows. Symptom: shuffle service overload. Fix: enable spark.shuffle.service.enabled.
fields.correctAnswer: FULL OUTER is not supported by AQE skew handling. Customer_type is pre-skewed; FULL OUTER produces hot partitions AQE cannot split. Executors OOM, tasks fail 4 times. Fix: INNER + null-handling.
fields.rationale: Outer join compatibility with AQE governs whether skew handling can engage.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Names a real concern (date scope) but it does not produce per-task OOM.
Option C: Dismisses the alert.

fields.label: Q5 — Bug #5 — Line 44 (the UDF receives customer_type_salted instead of customer_type). What is the production-correctness bug?
options: No bug — engineer's intent is per-region totals, not per-customer-type. Salt-then-aggregate is correctly collapsed by region. Pipeline produces the right output for the stated goal.
customer_type_salted is passed instead of customer_type. Dict has only unsalted keys; every salted lookup misses. Revenue is wrong for 40% of rows. Fix: pass col('customer_type').
groupBy by region collapses the salt buckets before the salt has served its purpose; the salt should be removed before the per-region groupBy via 2-stage aggregate.
broadcast(customers) is preserved through the aggregation, so per-region totals incorrectly carry customer-master columns. Fix: .drop() those columns before groupBy.
fields.correctAnswer: customer_type_salted is passed instead of customer_type. Dict has only unsalted keys; every salted lookup misses. Revenue is wrong for 40% of rows. Fix: pass col('customer_type').
fields.rationale: , RESIDENTIAL_3) to the UDF.The dict on line 41 only has unsalted keys ('RESIDENTIAL').0.85).
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats per-region as the only output.Per-row revenue is wrong before aggregation.
